phonemes.desc: Written sqr; conventionally vocalised “Sokar”. The name may mean “the mysterious one”.
The falcon god of the Memphis necropolis, patron of the royal tomb-workers.

kin.label: Fused

pronunciation.note: His festival, the raising of the Djed-pillar, was performed at the opening of the earth’s year.

domains.title: God of the Memphis Necropolis, the Mound of Creation
domains.subtitle: The Mysterious One, Patron of the Tomb-Makers
domains.lead: Sqr — Sokar — is the falcon of the Memphite dead: lord of the desert necropolis west of Memphis, master of its legendary tomb and workshop, and keeper of the mound where creation is annually re-declared. In him the arts of the dead — mummification, metalwork, resurrection — found their most ancient patron.

cards.name: Lord of Rostjau
cards.desc: Sovereign of the necropolis region (Rosetjau) and its royal tomb workshops.

cards.name: The Falcon of Silver
cards.desc: His shrine was the Henu barque with the head of a falcon — the solar-funeral vessel of the Memphite dead.

cards.name: Master of Metalworkers
cards.desc: The tomb’s goldsmiths and smiths of sacred metal worked under his protection.

cards.name: The Djed Mound
cards.desc: His festival raised the Djed-pillar on the primeval mound — Osiris’ spine set upright in the earth.

mythology.lead: Sokar’s mythology is the theology of the Memphite necropolis as a creation-site. The desert west of Memphis — Rostjau, ‘the passage of the ram-heads’ — was, in his cult, the primeval mound where the work of resurrection is endlessly performed. With Ptah and Osiris he forms the great funerary trinity that carried Egyptian hopes of afterlife through two millennia.

myths.title: The Mound in the Necropolis
myths.text: Sokar’s domain was not merely burial-ground but cosmogram: the Memphite desert’s hillocks were read as the world’s first mound rising from Nun. His priests raised the Djed-pillar there each year — Osiris’ backbone set upright in Sokar’s earth — and the world’s order was reaffirmed at the threshold of the dead.

myths.title: The Voyage of the Funerary Falcon
myths.text: The Sokar-festival’s climax was the procession of the Henu: a ship-shaped shrine on a sledge, its prow a falcon-head, drawn around the Memphite walls at dawn. The dead of the necropolis were imagined sailing with him; the barque’s circuit through the desert gates was the afterlife’s rehearsal.

myths.title: The Memphite Trinity
myths.text: As Memphis’ theology systematised, Sokar fused with Ptah the creator and Osiris the resurrected into the compound Ptah-Sokar-Osiris — the complete god of the dead: the one who makes, the one who is buried, the one who rises. Late-period amulets and coffins carry the triple name as a single guarantee.

myths.title: Patron of the Workmen
myths.text: The royal necropolis workmen — the draughtsmen, carpenters and goldsmiths who built the Valley of the Kings — placed their craft under Sokar. Ostraca from Deir el-Medina invoke him as the foreman of the ultimate workshop, where every artefact is made to outlast eternity.

lore.syncretism: Sokar is a study in controlled fusion: with Ptah as Ptah-Sokar, with Osiris as Sokar-Osiris, and in the full Memphite formula as all three. The Greeks rendered him Sarapis’ deepest Egyptian stratum — the Apis bull’s Memphite necropolis was Sokar’s ground long before Serapis was imagined.
lore.culturalLegacy: His festival ship, the Henu, survives in hundreds of amulets and in the standard late coffin-foot vignette; and the Djed-raising rite he hosted became the emblematic ‘erection of Osiris’ celebrated at the New Year across Egypt. The Memphite trinity remains the textbook example of Egyptian god-compounding done to completion.
lore.extendedMeditation: Sqr: a name whose very root, in Egyptian, whispers ‘do not ask’. He is the mysterious one, and his restoration honours that — three plain letters that decline to explain themselves, guarding the west as they have since before the pyramids.

sources.name: Memphite funerary liturgies and the Shabaka Stone tradition

lore.archaeology: His Memphite shrines are largely lost beneath the cultivation, but the Henu-barque amulets by the thousand, the Djed-pillar iconography, and the Saqqara Serapeum’s older strata preserve his cult’s materiality. The Late Period shaft-tombs of the sacred animals at Saqqara ran through ground his priests had held for millennia.
lore.cult: The Sokar-festival in the fourth month of inundation opened with the Djed-raising and closed with the Henu procession around the Memphite walls — a civic event as much as a funerary one. Smiths and tomb-workers kept his small cults in the necropolis villages; his was a guild-god’s religion of craft and precision.
lore.iconography: A falcon-headed man, or the falcon upon its Henu sledge-shrine with high prow; wings spread in protection over the necropolis. The Djed-pillar and the was-sceptre accompany him, and his funerary colour is the black of the fertile necropolis earth.
lore.reception: Through the Sarapis connection, Sokar’s Memphite ground became part of the ancient world’s most exported cult; through the Djed-raising, his image passed into the Hermetic and alchemical imagination as the spine of the world set upright — the axis of resurrection.
